newsitem.title: MONACO: Capital markets set to enter reinsurance - industry.
newsitem.headline: Capital markets set to enter reinsurance - industry.

text.p: Billions of dollars from the world's capital markets will increasingly be used to back alternatives to traditional reinsurance policies for high-risk business, industry experts said.

Reinsurance executives at the industry's annual rendezvous in Monte Carlo were told on Tuesday how a series of product ideas is now being developed, such as risk bonds issued by institutional investors, including life insurance and pension funds and banks.

Wolf Bauer of Munich Re said capital markets could complement traditional reinsurance in several areas. Bauer pointed out that in the U.S. alone there is around $19 trillion capital available daily, with an average fluctuation of $133 billion. This dwarfs the $210 billion surplus available in the U.S. reinsurance market.

The most expensive insured loss in the U.S. would be an earthquake in northern California or perhaps the New Madrid fault. A $75 billion loss would devastate the insurance and reinsurance industry, whereas the capital markets could absorb it without significant disruption.

"The traditional insurance and reinsurance markets have undergone major changes. The distinct borders between them and the financial markets are likely to erode to some extent in the future. Therefore banks and reinsurers will depend more on each other, especially when it comes to the successful exploitation and combination of skills and know-how," said Bauer.

Development of this field has been led by moves such as the launching of catastrophe futures and options trading in 1993 by the Chicago Board of Trade. It could lead to company bank overdraft facilities being replaced by the issuing of corporate bonds.
Dr Jurgen Zech, chairman of the Cologne-based Gerling insurance group, said capital market products would not push conventional insurance products out of the market.

"There is an unequivocal tendency among all players in the traditional insurance market to stick to relations and systems that have grown in years. This is partly due to the fact that conventional insurance has proved its value and its costs over many years."
Hady Wakefield, chairman of reinsurance broker Guy Carpenter, said, "If the capital markets are to play a part there must be recognition of insurance risk as a specific asset class.

"Our research shows that catastrophe bonds can show attractive anticipated returns relative to comparable risk securities, as well as providing reasonably priced insurance. Thus one should expect considerable interest from insurers and reinsurers once investors enter the market in a significant way," he said.
Andrew Alper, a partner with investment bank Goldman Sachs, dismissed doubts that non-insurance practitioners would be able to develop a realistic pricing strategy.
"Our view is that once the capital markets are comfortable in assessing risk they will be competitive at pricing," he said.
Wakefield said he doubted that Lloyd's of London would be able to take advantage of such changes to the reinsurance industry.

"I do not believe it will be in a position to play the meaningful role that it should because of its constitution. Capital market involvement does not favour the Lloyd's annual venture, nor do I believe that unlimited liability is appropriate today. Clients want to see exactly what assets are behind the policy they are buying," said Wakefield.

"Thus I believe that if syndicates at Lloyd's want to play a significant role in tomorrow's reinsurance business, the sooner they go wholly corporate and the sooner they account on a one year continuous basis the better." he said.
-- Gordon Mackenzie, Reuters Insurance News +377 93 50 65 00 ext 88031
